items.stem: Explain why it is important for a business to classify costs as fixed or variable.
items.answer: It allows marginal costing, break-even analysis and decision making (e.g. special orders), because only variable costs change with output.
items.markingKey: Behaviour with output [1]; use in decisions/break-even [1] [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between direct costs and indirect costs, giving an example of each.
items.answer: Direct costs can be identified with a unit (e.g. raw materials); indirect costs cannot and are shared (e.g. factory rent).
items.markingKey: Direct + example [1]; indirect + example [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the method used to price material issues affects both product cost and closing inventory.
items.answer: The same total cost is split between issues (charged to production) and the balance (closing inventory); a method that charges more to issues leaves less in inventory.
items.markingKey: Total cost divided [1]; trade-off between issues and inventory [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain one advantage of FIFO for valuing material issues.
items.answer: It is logical (oldest materials used first), easy to apply, and closing inventory is at recent prices; it is acceptable under IAS 2.
items.markingKey: Advantage explained [2]

items.stem: Explain why a guaranteed minimum wage is often included in a piece-rate scheme.
items.answer: It protects workers when output is low for reasons beyond their control (machine breakdowns, material shortages), and may be legally required.
